run.name: FDGA 2026 ALARM Benchmark — Congress
run.description: ALARM Project SMC ensemble for Georgia congress redistricting. Re-scored with the 2018–2024 five-election composite (2018 Governor, 2020 President, 2021 Warnock Senate Runoff, 2022 Governor + Senate avg, 2024 President) to match the GerryChain benchmark electoral baseline. Non-partisan metrics (compactness, splits, minority VAP) are from the original ALARM stats CSV (ALARM Project via Harvard Dataverse, doi:10.7910/DVN/SLCD3E).

dem_seats.label: Seat–Vote Proportionality
dem_seats.headline: Does the seat count reflect how people actually voted?
dem_seats.description: In a fair map, the share of seats each party wins should reflect its share of statewide votes. This metric counts districts projected to lean Democratic based on each plan's vote patterns — not as a partisan goal, but as a measuring stick for proportionality. The histogram shows how many Democratic-leaning seats thousands of neutrally drawn alternative maps produce. If the enacted map falls far from this range, lines were likely drawn to systematically over- or under-represent one party.
dem_seats.takeaway: The enacted map produces 5 Democratic-leaning seats — at the 34th percentile, below the neutral median of 6 (range: 5–7). This is within the normal range for neutral maps, suggesting a structural seat advantage for Republicans.

formula_info.detail: dem_2pv_d = Σ dem_votes_vtd / Σ (dem_votes_vtd + rep_votes_vtd) for all VTDs in district d
formula_info.data_source: VTD composite — 2018–2024 five-election average (2018 Gov, 2020 Pres, 2021 Warnock runoff, 2022 Gov+Senate avg, 2024 Pres)

efficiency_gap.label: Wasted Votes Balance
efficiency_gap.headline: Are both parties' votes equally effective at winning representation?
efficiency_gap.description: Every election produces 'wasted' votes — votes cast in losing districts (all wasted) and surplus votes beyond what was needed to win (also wasted). A fair map wastes votes at roughly equal rates for both parties. The Efficiency Gap measures the difference: a positive value means one party's votes are being wasted at a higher rate than the other's — a sign that district lines are concentrating or dispersing that party's voters artificially. Developed by Stephanopoulos & McGhee; cited in federal gerrymandering litigation.
efficiency_gap.takeaway: The enacted map's efficiency gap (0.172) is above the neutral median (0.099), at the 96th percentile — outside the normal range for neutral maps. Democratic votes are wasted at a higher rate, giving Republicans a structural advantage in translating votes to seats.

formula_info.formula: (Σ wasted_dem − Σ wasted_rep) / Σ total_votes  across all districts
formula_info.detail: wasted_dem = excess Dem votes beyond 50%+1 in Dem wins + all Dem votes in Dem losses; symmetric for Rep

mean_median.label: Vote Distribution Symmetry
mean_median.headline: Does each party need the same number of votes to win a district?
mean_median.description: The Mean-Median difference reveals whether one party's votes are systematically spread more efficiently across districts than the other's. When one party wins many districts by modest margins while the other piles up large majorities in fewer districts, the map gives the first party a structural seat advantage — even when both parties receive equal votes statewide. A value near zero means both parties convert votes to seats at roughly the same rate. A large deviation in either direction is a signal of asymmetric voter distribution — often a hallmark of gerrymandering.
mean_median.takeaway: The mean–median difference (0.069) is above the neutral median (0.039), at the 99th percentile — an extreme outlier — this result would occur by chance in fewer than 1 in 40 neutral maps. Democratic voters are disproportionately concentrated in fewer districts, giving Republicans a more efficient geographic spread of support.

formula_info.detail: Positive → Dem votes distributed less efficiently across districts (Republican structural advantage). Negative → reverse.

comp_seats.label: Electoral Competitiveness
comp_seats.headline: How many districts give voters a meaningful choice?
comp_seats.description: A competitive district is one where the outcome is genuinely uncertain — where the margin between the two parties is within 5 percentage points of 50/50. Competitive districts force elected officials to be responsive to a broad range of constituents, not just their party base. Maps designed to protect incumbents — whether Republican or Democratic — tend to minimize competitiveness. This metric asks whether the enacted map produces fewer competitive districts than neutral alternatives would.
comp_seats.takeaway: The enacted map has just 2 competitive district(s) — fewer than 88% of neutral maps. Most voters live in districts where outcomes are predetermined.

formula_info.detail: A district is competitive if the two-party Democratic share falls within ±competitive_margin of 50%

maj_black.label: Black Community Representation
maj_black.headline: Do Black voters have the opportunity to elect representatives of their choice?
maj_black.description: This counts districts where Black Voting Age Population (BVAP) makes up at least 20% of total Voting Age Population — the influence/coalition threshold. Under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, mapmakers must not draw lines that dilute minority communities' ability to elect their preferred candidates. The histogram shows how many influence-level Black districts thousands of neutrally drawn alternative maps produce. Standard Princeton symmetric grading is used: both unusually low and unusually high counts are flagged relative to the neutral ensemble. Uses 2020 Census PL 94-171 headcounts (not ACS estimates).
maj_black.takeaway: The enacted map has 10 majority-Black district(s), within the typical range for neutral maps (10–11).

formula_info.detail: Uses 2020 Census PL 94-171 headcounts (Table P4, P0040006 NH Black alone / P0040001 Total VAP). Headcounts — not ACS estimates.

min_coal.label: Minority Coalition Representation
min_coal.headline: Do communities of color collectively hold electoral influence?
min_coal.description: This counts districts where non-white Voting Age Population makes up at least 20% of total VAP — communities of color collectively hold influence even when no single racial group holds a majority. Standard Princeton symmetric grading is used: both unusually low and unusually high counts relative to the neutral ensemble are flagged. Uses 2020 Census PL 94-171 headcounts (not ACS estimates).
min_coal.takeaway: The enacted map has 14 minority-coalition district(s) — more than most neutral alternatives. Communities of color have strong collective electoral influence.

formula_info.detail: Combined non-white VAP share (1 − NH White fraction). A minority-coalition district includes multiple racial groups, none individually a majority.

polsby_popper.label: Compactness (Polsby-Popper)
polsby_popper.headline: Are district shapes compact and geographically coherent?
polsby_popper.description: The Polsby-Popper score measures shape compactness (ratio of area to perimeter²). Scores near 1 indicate circular, compact districts. Oddly shaped districts can signal that lines were drawn to include or exclude specific communities.
polsby_popper.takeaway: Enacted value: 0.249. Neutral median: 0.231 (range: 0.194–0.277). At the 77th percentile — within the normal range for neutral maps.

county_splits.label: County Integrity
county_splits.headline: Are natural community boundaries being respected?
county_splits.description: The number of counties divided across two or more districts. Fewer splits means more communities of interest are kept intact.
county_splits.takeaway: Enacted value: 15.000. Neutral median: 10.000 (range: 7.000–12.000). At the 100th percentile — an extreme outlier — this result would occur by chance in fewer than 1 in 40 neutral maps.

muni_splits.label: Municipal Integrity
muni_splits.headline: Are cities and towns being kept whole?
muni_splits.description: The number of cities and municipalities divided across different districts. Fewer splits means residents share a single representative for local concerns.
muni_splits.takeaway: The enacted map splits 16 cities and municipalities — more than 100% of neutral maps (typical range: 3–11). This is an extreme outlier: the enacted map cracks far more urban communities than geography-driven redistricting would produce. Dividing cities dilutes their collective political voice and reduces constituent access to a single local representative.

_partisan_fairness.label: Partisan Fairness
_partisan_fairness.description: Assessed using the Princeton Gerrymandering Project's ensemble test against a composite partisan benchmark averaging 5 elections: 2018 Governor, 2020 President, 2021 Warnock Senate Runoff, 2022 Governor + Senate (averaged), and 2024 President. Third-party candidates are excluded (2-party vote shares only). The ENSEMBLE test checks whether the enacted map falls within the normal range (5th–95th percentile) of outcomes for thousands of randomly drawn alternative maps drawn without partisan intent. Ensemble: ✗ FAIL — the enacted map produces unusually partisan outcomes compared to neutral alternatives. Note: The normative (cube-law symmetry) test requires a partisan bias metric not available in GerryChain runs — it is conservatively set to Pass.

_overall.label: Overall
_overall.description: The Overall grade summarizes how the enacted map compares to thousands of alternative maps drawn without partisan intent. It starts from the Partisan Fairness grade and adjusts upward if the map is unusually competitive (more competitive districts than typical), or downward if it has zero competitive districts. Geographic quality (compactness, county splits) is not yet available for GerryChain runs. An A means the enacted map performs as well as or better than neutral alternatives — it does not stand out as gerrymandered. An F means the map produces outcomes that are highly unlikely to occur by chance in a fair redistricting process.
